config.title: Test Async Component

intro.title: Test Async Component
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React component that fetches and displays a list of users from a mock API. You will learn how to test asynchronous behavior in React components using React Testing Library and Jest. The core concepts involve mocking API calls, handling loading and error states, and writing assertions for asynchronous UI updates. You will work with TypeScript, async/await, and common testing utilities to ensure your component behaves correctly under different network conditions.
intro.usecase: Testing async components is essential for building reliable data-driven interfaces in production applications. This pattern appears when testing dashboard widgets that fetch live metrics, search filters that query APIs, or user profile panels that load external data. Developers use these tests to ensure components handle loading states, error scenarios, and successful data rendering correctly before deployment. Without proper async testing, applications risk displaying broken UI or failing silently when backend services are slow or unavailable.

objectives: Apply async/await syntax to handle asynchronous operations within React components.
Implement loading state management to display user feedback during data fetching.
Use error state handling to gracefully display error messages when API calls fail.
Construct mock API service functions to simulate asynchronous data retrieval.
Execute conditional rendering to display different UI states based on loading, error, and data conditions.
Define TypeScript interfaces to type-check the structure of fetched data.
Invoke useEffect hooks to trigger asynchronous operations on component mount.
Control component re-renders by properly managing state updates within async functions.
Utilize try-catch blocks to handle potential errors in asynchronous operations.
Return appropriate JSX elements for each possible component state (loading, error, success).
Assign fetched data to component state to trigger UI updates when operations complete.
Access component state values to conditionally render content based on the current state.

steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing React and useState
import React, { useState } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use.
successCriteria: The code should include an import statement that imports React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState, which are essential for building React components with state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the import statement might be incomplete or incorrect. Make sure to import both React and useState from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. You need to import React and useState from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main component function
steps.instruction: Create a function component named TestAsyncComponent that returns a JSX.Element.
steps.hint: Define a function with the name TestAsyncComponent that returns some JSX content. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Create the TestAsyncComponent function component here
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named TestAsyncComponent is defined and returns JSX.
successCriteria: The component is named TestAsyncComponent, returns JSX, and has a return type of JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the TestAsyncComponent function component with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your component is named exactly 'TestAsyncComponent' and returns JSX with the correct return type annotation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component definition doesn't match the requirements. Check that you've named it 'TestAsyncComponent' and it returns JSX with proper TypeScript typing.

steps.title: Initialize loading state
steps.instruction: Inside your TestAsyncComponent function, use the useState hook to create a boolean state variable called 'loading' with an initial value of false.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook you imported earlier. Remember to use TypeScript generics to specify the type as boolean.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of creating a boolean loading state
const [loading, setLoading] = useState<boolean>(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have a loading state variable initialized to false using useState with proper TypeScript typing.
successCriteria: The code must include: 1) useState hook call, 2) boolean type annotation using <boolean>, 3) initial value of false, 4) proper array destructuring with 'loading' and 'setLoading' variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the loading state with proper TypeScript typing. This boolean state will help track when your async operation is in progress.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check: 1) Did you use useState<boolean>(false)? 2) Did you destructure both 'loading' and 'setLoading'? 3) Is the initial value exactly 'false'?
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on just this step. You need to call useState<boolean>(false) inside your component and destructure the result into [loading, setLoading]. Make sure you're using the useState hook you imported earlier.

steps.title: Initialize data state
steps.instruction: Inside your component, initialize a data state variable using useState. The state should start as null and be typed to hold either null or a string.
steps.hint: Use useState with a generic type like <string | null> to define the state type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a typed state that can be null or string
const [data, setData] = useState<string | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a data state variable initialized with null that can later store string values.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call with generic type <string | null> and initial value null, assigning the state variable and setter to appropriate names.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized a typed data state that can be null or string.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your useState is typed correctly (e.g., <string | null>) and initialized with null.
steps.feedbackWrong: The data state initialization is missing or incorrect. Make sure to use useState with the proper type and initial value.

steps.title: Initialize error state
steps.instruction: Initialize an error state variable using useState, starting with null as its initial value. This state will hold either null or a string error message.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with a generic type to specify that the state can be null or string.
steps.analogousExample:
// Initialize error state
const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have an error state variable initialized to null, ready to store error messages.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the error state with the correct type. This will allow you to track and display error messages when needed.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using useState with the correct generic type (string | null) and initializing it to null. Also verify the variable names match the expected pattern.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. You need to initialize an error state variable using useState. The state should start as null and be able to hold either null or a string value.

steps.title: Create the fetchData async function
steps.instruction: Inside your TestAsyncComponent, create an async function named fetchData that returns Promise<void>. This function will later simulate fetching data.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword before the function declaration. The function should return a Promise<void> type.
steps.expectedOutcome: An async function named fetchData that returns Promise<void> is added to the component.
successCriteria: The code contains an async function named fetchData with return type Promise<void> defined inside the component.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the fetchData async function. This function will be used to simulate API calls in the next steps.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is async and returns Promise<void>. Check the function name and return type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData async function wasn't created correctly. Remember to use the async keyword and specify Promise<void> as the return type.

steps.title: Implement fetchData loading state logic
steps.instruction: Inside the fetchData function, set the loading state to true at the beginning of the function to indicate the async operation has started.
steps.hint: Use the setLoading function you already have to update the loading state to true.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData function will now properly indicate when an async operation starts by setting loading to true.
successCriteria: The fetchData function should contain setLoading(true) as the first statement inside its body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've correctly set the loading state to true at the start of the async operation. This gives users immediate feedback that something is happening.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure setLoading(true) is inside the fetchData function body and is the first statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData function should begin by setting loading to true. Look for where you can call setLoading(true) inside the function.

steps.title: Implement fetchData async simulation
steps.instruction: Inside the fetchData function, add a setTimeout that simulates a 1-second async operation. The setTimeout should contain the logic that will eventually set the data or error states.
steps.hint: Use setTimeout with a 1000ms delay. Inside the callback, you'll add the simulation logic in the next steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData function now includes a setTimeout that will simulate a 1-second async delay before executing any further logic.
successCriteria: setTimeout callback is defined (can be empty for now)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the setTimeout to simulate an async delay. This is the foundation for the async simulation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've added setTimeout with a 1000ms delay inside the fetchData function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData function should include a setTimeout with 1000ms delay to simulate async behavior.

steps.title: Implement fetchData success handling
steps.instruction: Inside the setTimeout callback in your fetchData function, set the data state to 'Async data loaded!' and set loading to false.
steps.hint: Remember to call both setData and setLoading inside the setTimeout callback.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData function now handles successful async operations by updating the data state and resetting loading.
successCriteria: The setTimeout callback should include setData('Async data loaded!') and setLoading(false).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the success handling logic for the async operation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure both setData and setLoading are called inside the setTimeout callback.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're setting data to 'Async data loaded!' and loading to false inside the setTimeout callback.

steps.title: Return the main container div
steps.instruction: Return a div element from the TestAsyncComponent function. This will serve as the main container for your component's UI.
steps.hint: The component should return JSX. Add a return statement with a div element.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now returns a div element, which will be the foundation for adding UI elements in subsequent steps.
successCriteria: The component returns a div element as JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully returned a div element from your component. This provides the basic structure for your UI.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but make sure you're returning a div element from the component function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component doesn't seem to return a div element. Remember to add a return statement with a div tag.

steps.title: Add the fetch button with onClick handler
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add a button element with an onClick handler that calls the fetchData function. The button should be disabled when the loading state is true.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with onClick={fetchData} and disabled={loading} attributes.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a button with onClick and disabled attributes
<button onClick={handleClick} disabled={isLoading}>
  Fetch Data
</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button that triggers the fetchData function when clicked and becomes disabled during loading.
successCriteria: The button element must be inside the returned JSX, have an onClick handler set to fetchData, and have a disabled attribute set to the loading state variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added a button that will trigger the async operation and properly disables during loading.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a button, but it's missing either the onClick handler or the disabled attribute. Make sure both are included.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button element is missing or incorrectly implemented. Check that you've added a <button> with onClick={fetchData} and disabled={loading}.

steps.title: Display loading, data, and error states
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add conditional rendering to display the loading indicator when loading is true, show the data when it exists, and show the error message when there's an error.
steps.hint: Use the loading, data, and error state variables with conditional operators (like ternary or logical &&) to render different UI elements.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will conditionally display UI elements based on the current state values.
successCriteria: The code should include conditional rendering for all three states (loading, data, error) using the existing state variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added conditional rendering to display the loading indicator, data, and error messages based on the component state.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some conditional rendering, but make sure to handle all three states (loading, data, and error) with appropriate UI elements.
steps.feedbackWrong: The conditional rendering for the three states is missing or incorrect. Check that you're using the loading, data, and error state variables to conditionally render UI elements.
